title: Diagonalizable and unipotent product decomposition of a commutative algebraic group
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], and let $G$ be a commutative affine $k$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. There are closed subgroup schemes $D,U\subseteq G$ [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup] such that multiplication is an isomorphism of $k$-group schemes $U\times_kD\xrightarrow{\sim}G$ [def-pc-fibre-product]. The group $D$ is diagonalizable: for some finitely generated abelian group $M$, it is isomorphic to $\operatorname{Spec}k[M]$, where $k[M]$ has basis $e_m$, multiplication $e_me_l=e_{m+l}$, comultiplication $e_m\mapsto e_m\otimes e_m$, counit $e_m\mapsto1$ and antipode $e_m\mapsto e_{-m}$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum, lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property]. For some $n\geq1$ there is a closed group embedding $U\hookrightarrow U_{n,k}$ [def-weil-closed-immersion, def-sc-general-linear-group], where $U_{n,k}(R)$ is the group under matrix multiplication of upper triangular $n\times n$ matrices over the commutative $k$-algebra $R$ with all diagonal entries $1$. These assertions require neither smoothness nor connectedness of $G$; the trivial group permits $D=U=1$ and $n=1$.

source.place: Theorem 16.13(b), printed p.328 (over the perfect field k); Theorems 12.8--12.9, printed pp.233--234, and Section 12.14, printed p.236 (multiplicative type over an algebraically closed field is diagonalizable); Theorem 14.5(a),(b), printed p.281 (unitriangular realization of unipotence).

proof.text: Take the identity subgroup $T=1\subseteq G$. It is closed: its coordinate map $k[G]\to k$ is a $k$-algebra map, hence surjective since it contains every scalar, so the affine criterion of [def-weil-closed-immersion] applies. It is central and is the rank-zero split torus. Apply [lem-sfb-central-torus-faithful-weight-blocks] with $F=k$, $H=G$, $T=1$ and $r=0$. Its hypotheses require only an affine finite-type group and a central closed split torus, not smoothness or connectedness. Retain its nonzero finite-dimensional $k$-vector space $V$ and its closed-immersion homomorphism $\rho:G\hookrightarrow\operatorname{GL}(V)$. Put $n=\dim_k V\geq1$.

source.place: Theorem 4.9 and Corollary 4.10, printed p.87; specialization of the existing faithful weight-block lemma to the trivial torus.

proof.text: Construct a complete $G$-stable flag $0=V_0\subset V_1\subset\cdots\subset V_n=V$, with $\dim V_j=j$, by induction on $j$. If $j<n$, the quotient $V/V_j$ has a rational $G$-action: in a basis beginning with a basis of $V_j$, the matrices of $\rho$ and their inverses have zero lower-left block over every $k$-algebra, and their lower-right blocks give mutually inverse matrices on the quotient. Their entries are regular functions, and the group multiplication equation passes to that block. Apply [lem-sfb-commutative-group-representation-eigenline] to this nonzero finite-dimensional quotient. Its field is algebraically closed and its acting group is the same commutative affine finite-type $G$. It supplies a $G$-stable line $L$ in $V/V_j$. Define $V_{j+1}$ as its inverse image. A lift of a nonzero vector of $L$ extends a basis of $V_j$, so $\dim V_{j+1}=j+1$. Over every $k$-algebra $A$, a vector in $A\otimes_kV_{j+1}$ has image in $A\otimes_kL$; this image stays there under $G(A)$, proving stability. The tensor identifications here follow directly by extending bases of the indicated subspaces. At $j=n$ dimension gives $V_n=V$.

source.place: Proposition 16.2(a)⇒(b), printed p.325, flag induction; the existing eigenline lemma supplies the scheme-theoretic commutative input, without using Corollary 16.14 as a black box.

proof.text: Choose a basis of $V$ adapted to this flag. For every $k$-algebra $A$ all matrices $\rho_A(g)$ are upper triangular, since their first $j$ columns preserve $A\otimes_kV_j$. In particular the lower-triangular coordinate entries vanish on the universal point $g\in G(k[G])$, so the morphism factors through the upper triangular closed subgroup $B_n\subseteq\operatorname{GL}_{n,k}$. This factor is a closed immersion: the surjection $k[\operatorname{GL}_n]\to k[G]$ for $\rho$ factors through its quotient by the lower-triangular entries, which is $k[B_n]$, and the induced map is still surjective [def-weil-closed-immersion, def-sc-general-linear-group]. Changing basis conjugates matrices by a fixed invertible matrix, with inverse conjugation, so preserves the original surjectivity. Identify $G$ with this closed subgroup $J\subseteq B_n$; all subsequent subgroups and morphisms are transported along this group-scheme isomorphism.

source.place: Proposition 16.2(b)⇒(c), printed p.325; affine coordinate verification of the factorization into the triangular group.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-triangular-diagonal-kernel] to $J\subseteq B_n$ over the algebraically closed field $k$. It gives $U=J\cap U_{n,k}$, a closed normal subgroup with its closed unitriangular embedding, the represented quotient $q:J\to Q=J/U$, a closed immersion $Q\hookrightarrow\mathbf G_m^n$, and a group-scheme section $s:Q\to J$. It also gives the scheme isomorphism $\alpha:U\times_kQ\to J$, $(u,a)\mapsto u\,s(a)$. These are precisely the conclusions of the cited node for arbitrary closed triangular subgroups; its smooth-connected clause is not used. The same $n\geq1$ therefore already supplies the required closed embedding for $U$.

source.place: Proposition 16.2(c)⇒(d), printed p.325, and Theorem 16.26(a), printed pp.332–333.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-split-torus-subgroups-diagonalizable] to the closed subgroup $Q\subseteq\mathbf G_m^n$. It gives a finitely generated abelian group $M$ and an isomorphism $Q\simeq\operatorname{Spec}k[M]$ with exactly the basis, multiplication, comultiplication, counit and antipode in the statement. For every $k$-algebra $A$, $q_A s_A=\operatorname{id}$, so $s_A$ is injective. The source $Q$ and target $J$ are affine group schemes of finite type, so [lem-sfb-geometric-unipotence-faithful-closed-immersion] applies to $s$ and proves that $s$ is a closed immersion. Let $D\subseteq J$ be this closed subgroup, identified with $Q$ by $s$. Thus $D$ is diagonalizable with the same group algebra and is a subgroup scheme, rather than only an abstract quotient.

source.place: Theorems 12.8–12.9, printed pp.233–234, for the diagonalizable presentation; Corollary 3.35, printed p.75, for the section as a closed immersion.

proof.text: Under $Q\simeq D$, the scheme isomorphism $\alpha$ is multiplication $U\times_kD\to J$. It is a group homomorphism: for every $k$-algebra $A$, commutativity of $J(A)$ gives $(u\,s(a))(v\,s(b))=uv\,s(ab)$, which is the image of the componentwise product $(uv,ab)$. The inverse of a scheme isomorphism that is a group homomorphism is again a group homomorphism: apply its inverse to the multiplication equation. Transporting $U,D$ back along $G\simeq J$ gives the asserted isomorphism of $k$-group schemes. For $G=1$ choose $U=D=1$, $M=0$ and $n=1$. The construction used arbitrary algebra-valued actions throughout; in particular it did not assume that field-valued points detect a subgroup.

source.place: Theorem 16.26(a), printed pp.332–333, specialized to a commutative triangular group; elementary direct-product assembly giving Theorem 16.13(b).

proof_origin.place: Assembly using Theorem 4.9 (p.87), Proposition 16.2 (p.325), Theorem 16.26(a) (pp.332–333), and Theorems 12.8–12.9 (pp.233–234). This proves the statement of Theorem 16.13(b) via existing triangular-group nodes, rather than repeating its maximal-multiplicative-subgroup proof.
